chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
title: Studio band boys: Freddie the Freeloader, Larry and Onesta Reese
summary: They remember colorful band boys of the New York recording scene such as Freddie the Freeloader and Onesta Reese.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Now who do you think was the most popular band boy, that everybody just loved and everybody knew, and he was not even in one hundredth of the class of Rudolph? Can you think of who it is?
No, let me think ...
Back to our recording era and that -- he was with every band.
Oh, uh ... Freddie.
Freddie the Freeloader! He was a character.
Oh, he was a character if there ever was one; Freddie the Freeloader.
Oh, he'd bring my bass in on a date and he'd sit there and he'd have a few tastes -- he'd be the first one at the bar; before you ordered yours, he had already ordered and he said it was on you.
Oh, yeah ... whoever named him Freddie
the Freeloader had him down pat; they really knew what they were talking about.
But I tell you, I really miss Freddie.
Oh, a lot of people miss Freddie.
Just to have him around, because he was a good laugh.
He was another character.

Oh, he'd be sitting in the recording studio and while we were working there like crazy, he'd be sitting there asleep, and somebody would say, 'I think this record is gonna be a hit because Freddie slept right through it!'
Oh boy, those were beautiful days.
You remember [Croop?]
Yes.
Whose band was he with?
He was with Charlie Shaver's band. Yeah, when you saw Charlie you saw Croop.
Oh, yeah.
What ever happend to Croop, man?
He's still around. I see him every once in awhile on Eighth Avenue.
Yeah?
I haven't seen him the last year or so, but I'm sure ... I haven't heard anything. Freddie's gone.
Yeah, Freddie passed on.
And then, Larry -- you remember Larry?
Oh yeah, Larry was another one.
Stood on the corner and made faces at all the ladies.

The last time I saw Larry, he was on the subway, and the police was getting ready to throw him off because he had slept on both ends of the subway --he was making a night of it, and the police threw him off the train at 50th Street.
Well, I think they took him away, because nobody has seen him since! These guys were almost part of the recording business, you know, just to see them?
Sure. Do you remember, when we used to all meet, before Charlie's got very popular, all the guys would go to the Turf.
And the classic band boy for the recording industry was Onesta Reese.
Onesta Reese.
The most remarkable little Italian gentleman that just took care of everybody's instruments. He was beautiful.
Oh, yeah, he was just beautiful. He couldn't speak too much Engls, but he could sure take care of things.
And he couldn't write, either, but he could memorize; he had 100 guys to take care of and he knew where they would be and he would have their instruments ready.
That's right -- yessir.
And these gentlemen will really be sorely missed, who were such a great part of our recording business.
I often think of those guys, you know, and the different times that we had together.
That's right, man; it was really beautiful.
